newsitem.title: USA: Egypt's fiscal prudence seen lasting - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Egypt's fiscal prudence seen lasting - S&P.

text.p: Expectations that Egypt's fiscal correction will continue over the next five years underpin a stable credit rating outlook for the country's new BBB-minus investment grade rating, Standard & Poor's said.

"Sound fiscal management has been and will continue to be a prerequisite for macroeconomic stability, increasing savings and achieving high growth rates," said Cem Karacadag, an associate director with S&P's sovereign ratings group.
Karacadag addressed new Egyptian ratings on Wednesday in a conference call.
S&P one week ago assigned its BBB-minus long-term and A3 short-term foreign currency credit ratings to the Arab Republic of Egypt with a stable outlook.

Egypt's general government deficits have been slashed to 1.3 percent of gross domestic product in the last fiscal year from 15 percent in 1991, Karacadag said, reflecting prudent cuts in capital spending and government subsidies.
The introduction of a general sales tax in 1993 also played a primary role in the fiscal turnaround, he said.
The deficit is targeted at 1.1 percent of GDP for the 1996-1997 fiscal year and should remain low through at least the year 2000, Karacadag said.

Other factors in S&P's stable outlook include high but favorably structured government debt. Also, Karacadag said government deposits in the banking system equal to 17 percent of GDP confer "significant financial flexibility."
Elsewhere, Karacadag noted the government's committment to privatization and trade globalization is essential to achieving microeconomic stability.
Success thus far has been found through price decontrol, interest rate and foreign exchange globalization -- all conspiring to remove price distortions in the Egyptian economy.
A declining rate of inflation and positive central bank monetary policies also bolster Egypt's economic outlook.

"The central bank's success in managing capital inflows so far and its policy of intervening to prevent an upward but not downward movement in the exchange rate mean that central bank reserves will not be depleted quickly and that future inflows will be matched by an increase in reserves," he said.
Risks to productivity gains stem from the country's public sector-dominated and relatively protected economy, he said.

But privatization and trade globalization should prosper as Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak is now committed to reform, Karacadag said. Mubarak is expected to be easily reelected once his term expires, he said, and any long-term effects of a potential assassination would be limited.
"The demonstrable rewards of macroeconomic prudence and the deepening consensus of the necessity of public sector rationalization should sustain the process" if Mubarak were assassinated, he said.
Should the transfer of ownership to the private sector grind to a halt, Karacadag said lower savings and investment would curb growth prospects and eventually ratings.
"This could threaten macroeconomic stabilty over the long-term and with it Egypt's credit standing," he said.
Unrest in the middle east may have an indirect impact on tourism and foreign investments, the analyst said.

Offsetting strengths are a weak export base and Egypt's dependence on a few export receipts, such as petroleum, gas, the Suez Canal and tourism, he said, adding that they are manageable and remote risks.
